cards.title: Group orders
cards.prompt: A food delivery app has a group order feature: one person starts an order, friends add their own items, and it's delivered together.
cards.success_prompt: How would you define success for group ordering?
cards.diagnosis_prompt: Group orders dropped twelve percent week over week. Walk me through how you'd investigate.
cards.twist: A change that lets the host pay for everyone lifts group orders five percent, but average order value drops four percent. Would you ship it?
brief_lines: One host, friends add items, one delivery
facts_if_asked: Group orders are about eight percent of all orders.
The drop started last Tuesday.
All orders overall are flat.
The drop is almost entirely on Android; iOS and web are flat.
Android app version five point three shipped last Monday, rolled out over two days.
In five point three, the share link opens the app store instead of the order for friends without the app.
No holidays or competitor promotions that week.
follow_ups: Counted how: group orders started, or completed?
Which segment would you cut first?
What would you check first, and why?
strong_answer_covers: Success: north star such as completed group orders per week, supporting metrics such as joiners per group and repeat hosts, a guardrail such as delivery time or order errors
Clarifies the definition and the timing of the drop
Checks data and logging first
Separates internal and external causes
Segments by platform, version, region, new versus returning
Finds the funnel step: hosts starting fine, joiners failing
Trade-off: compares revenue per group, long term retention and who pays, sets a threshold or tests it
Segments before naming a cause; makes the ship call

cards.title: Save for later
cards.prompt: A shopping app has a save for later button on product pages and in the cart.
cards.success_prompt: How would you define success for save for later?
cards.diagnosis_prompt: Purchases of saved items fell nine percent this month, while saves are up. What's going on?
cards.twist: Moving the save button next to checkout in the cart raises saves twenty percent, but cart conversion drops point six percentage points. Ship it?
brief_lines: Shopping app, save for later button
On product pages and in the cart
facts_if_asked: Saves are up fifteen percent month over month.
The saved items list moved from the home tab into the account menu three weeks ago.
Visits to the saved list are down thirty percent since then.
Price drop alerts for saved items still work.
Overall purchases are flat.
follow_ups: What does a healthy save look like?
Could saves going up be bad?
Where in the funnel is the drop?
strong_answer_covers: North star such as purchases from saved items, with adoption and return visits as supporting metrics
Guardrail: cart conversion not cannibalised
Notices saves up while purchases from saves fall: a return path problem
Looks for a product change near the start of the drop
Trade-off: values a lost checkout against future purchases from saves, proposes a test or a threshold
Does not treat the rise in saves as good news or every save as purchase intent

cards.title: Podcast north star
cards.prompt: A podcast app lets people follow shows, download episodes and listen in the app.
cards.success_prompt: Pick a north star metric for the app and the metrics that support it.
cards.diagnosis_prompt: Downloads are up eight percent this month, but listening minutes per listener fell seven percent. How would you investigate?
cards.twist: Autoplaying the next episode raises listening minutes six percent, but complaints about unwanted plays double. Ship it?
facts_if_asked: Monthly listeners are flat.
A new auto download setting turned on by default for new follows shipped five weeks ago.
Most of the new downloads are never played.
Listening minutes per listener are down most for people who follow more than ten shows.
Storage complaints are up.
follow_ups: Why that north star over downloads?
How would someone game your metric?
Is the drop real or a definition change?
strong_answer_covers: North star such as weekly listening minutes of retained listeners, not downloads
Explains how downloads can be gamed or inflated
Supporting metrics: follows that lead to listens, completion rate
Finds the auto download change and heavy followers as the segment
Trade-off: weighs minutes against trust, proposes an opt in or a test with a complaint threshold
Does not dismiss complaints because minutes went up

cards.title: Daily reminders
cards.prompt: A language learning app sends daily reminder notifications to keep learners practising.
cards.success_prompt: How would you define success for the daily reminder?
cards.diagnosis_prompt: Day seven retention for new learners dropped from thirty eight to thirty three percent over two weeks. Investigate.
cards.twist: A new, more urgent reminder lifts sessions six percent, but uninstalls rise point four percentage points. Ship it?
facts_if_asked: The drop is only for new learners; existing learners are flat.
A new onboarding flow added three screens two weeks ago.
Notification opt in for new learners fell from seventy to fifty one percent.
The opt in prompt moved from the first lesson to the end of onboarding.
Marketing spend and channels are unchanged.
follow_ups: Is the drop real, or a change in who signs up?
Which step of the new learner journey moved?
strong_answer_covers: Success: lessons completed after a reminder, with opt outs and uninstalls as guardrails
Checks data, then whether the mix of new users changed
Finds the onboarding change and the opt in drop
Explains the mechanism: fewer reminders, fewer return visits
Trade-off: values an uninstall against session gains over months, segments who uninstalls, tests frequency or tone
Checks seasonality instead of assuming it; does not ship on the session lift alone
